old: The Thule people are beginning to expand east from Alaska, displacing the Dorset.
new: The Thule culture is taking shape in coastal Alaska; its rapid eastward migration, which will displace the Dorset, begins only around 1200.
source: Friesen & Arnold (2008), 'The Timing of the Thule Migration', American Antiquity 73(3):527-538: no Thule occupation in the western Canadian Arctic before the 13th century, spread beginning c. 1200, summarised at https://historicalclimatology.com/features/what-made-the-thule-move-climate-and-culture-in-the-high-arctic ; consistent with the atlas's own Thule profile ('From about 1200 ...')

old: The Thule people, ancestors of the Inuit, are spreading eastward across the Canadian Arctic with dog sleds and skin boats, replacing the Dorset.
new: The Thule people, ancestors of the Inuit, are perfecting their whaling way of life with dog sleds and skin boats in Alaska, while the Dorset still hold the Canadian Arctic.
source: Friesen & Arnold 2008, American Antiquity 73(3):527-538 (Thule eastward spread no earlier than c. 1200), via https://historicalclimatology.com/features/what-made-the-thule-move-climate-and-culture-in-the-high-arctic

old: The Thule people have spread across the Arctic and are reaching Greenland, where they meet the Norse settlers. The Dorset culture is disappearing.
new: The Thule people are beginning a rapid migration east from Alaska and within a century will reach Greenland, where they meet the Norse settlers. The Dorset culture still holds the eastern Arctic, but not for long.
source: Friesen & Arnold 2008, American Antiquity 73(3):527-538, via https://historicalclimatology.com/features/what-made-the-thule-move-climate-and-culture-in-the-high-arctic ; Dorset persisted to c. 1300-1400 CE: https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/dorset-culture
